title: Knowledge was worship
hook: scholars studied the stars and the body for the sake of Allah

segments.voice: Yesterday, rise and fall: Ibn Khaldun's pattern of asabiyya, a bond that builds and comfort that loosens. Your line was unity builds. Did you pull one rope a little tighter? Day one thousand forty-nine.

Standing. Sitting. Lying on your side. The Qur'an describes people who remember God in all three positions, and then it adds one more thing they do: they consider the creation of the heavens and the earth. Remembering, and then looking hard at the world. Put side by side in one verse. Back through this year's history we've met astronomers, physicians, mapmakers, people who measured the sky and opened books on the eye. It's easy to file them under science, a different drawer from prayer. The verse doesn't seem to keep two drawers. Today: knowledge was worship.
screen: `STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN.` → `THEN: CONSIDER THE CREATION.` → `ONE DRAWER, NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse itself, near the close of the third surah. The people of understanding remember Allah standing, sitting and reclining, they consider the heavens and the earth, and what comes out of their mouths is praise. In Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." The study ends in worship. Second, the body. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet, peace be upon him, saying that God has not sent down a disease without sending down its cure. Some readers heard that as a promise and an assignment at once: the cure exists, so go and find it. Physicians in Muslim lands wrote on the eye, on fevers, on the heart, and some of them saw the search as service. Third, the same person. History keeps handing us people who don't fit one label. Ibn Rushd of Cordoba was a judge of Islamic law and a physician. Ibn Sina wrote a canon of medicine and also commentaries on chapters of the Qur'an. To them the line between a religious subject and a worldly one wasn't drawn where a modern school timetable draws it. Fourth, the intention. What turned study into worship wasn't the subject. A scholar of grammar could study for fame; a pharmacist could study for God. The tradition kept asking what the work was for. That's the lesson the history leaves on an ordinary desk: a spreadsheet, a textbook, an engine manual. Look hard enough, with the right reason, and the verse's last line is waiting at the end.
screen: `REMEMBER, CONSIDER, THEN PRAISE.` · `EVERY DISEASE HAS A CURE: GO FIND IT.` · `A JUDGE WHO WAS ALSO A PHYSICIAN.` · `THE INTENTION MAKES IT WORSHIP.` · then, large: `THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: study something for Him, or simply for its own sake if that's how you come to it. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing within reach and look at it the way an astronomer looks at a star. Your own hand works well. The lines across the palm, the joints, the pulse at the wrist you can feel with two fingers. Count nothing. Just look closer than you usually would, and notice how much is there that you didn't make. If you pray, you can end with the verse's own words: our Lord, You did not create this in vain. The bell holds the time.
Ilm, the Arabic word for knowledge, studied by people like Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd as a form of worship when the intention is right. Today's word.
Your line: study as prayer. Today, learn one real thing about how the body or the sky works, and before you start, say to yourself what it's for. Day one thousand forty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims often begin study with the name of God and a renewed intention, and the Qur'an's plea for more knowledge (20:114) is one some students say before a lesson.

fork.setup: you're a young physician who has just heard the hadith that God sent no disease without its cure. a fever is killing people in your town and nobody knows a remedy. what does the hadith suggest?
options: accept it; if a cure existed, someone would know it.
the cure exists; search for it.
fork.reveal: some readers heard the hadith as both a promise and an assignment: the cure is there to be found.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious people studied religion, and scientists studied the world.
what it means: in this history, studying the stars and the body could itself be a way of worship.
what a scholar hears: Qur'an 3:190–191 moves from remembering God to considering creation to praise, and Ibn Rushd sat as a judge of Islamic law while writing on medicine.
